what_it_does: When engineers design a microchip, they must test whether tiny manufacturing flaws — called faults — would cause the circuit to produce wrong outputs. For sequential circuits (chips that have memory of past states, like flip-flops that store a 0 or 1 between clock ticks), testing is especially slow because a fault's effect can be trapped inside feedback loops and take many clock cycles to propagate out. EPICS tackles this by splitting the circuit into its feedback loops (called strongly connected components, or SCCs — groups of logic gates where signals can cycle back on themselves) and handling simple loops differently from complex ones. It combines two simulation strategies: a compiled mode that bakes a simple loop's behavior directly into fast executable code, and an event-driven mode that only re-evaluates a gate when one of its inputs actually changes, avoiding wasted work. The claimed result is significantly faster fault simulation for large sequential circuits, though the exact speedup figures would need verification from the full paper.
